description: Spain puts its own conquests on trial: Sepúlveda's natural-slavery argument against Las Casas's eyewitness testimony. No verdict — but the question survived.
essential_question: Were the conquests in the Americas just?

key_terms.definition: The 1550-51 council debate at Valladolid, Spain, over whether Spain's conquest of the Americas was just.
Spanish theologian who argued from Aristotle that Indigenous peoples were natural slaves and conquest was a just war.
Dominican friar whose fifty years in the Indies grounded his eyewitness case that Indigenous peoples were rational and Spanish cruelty was the true barbarism.
Sepúlveda's Aristotelian claim that some peoples are born to be ruled.
The forced-labor grant system at stake in the debate; unabolished by it.
Protestant, especially English, use of Spanish-cruelty accounts to justify their own colonization.

learning_objectives: Contrast Sepúlveda's and Las Casas's positions in the Valladolid debate
Explain why the debate produced no verdict and what survived it
Connect the debate to the encomienda system and the Black Legend

presentation.tone: a teacher talking to a smart 16-year-old; plain, spoken, concrete

narration.text: In 1550, the most powerful empire on earth did something no empire had ever done. [beat] Spain put its own conquests on trial. In Valladolid, a council of theologians and lawyers met to answer a single question: was the conquest of the Americas just, or was it a crime?

beats.cue: A war that ends such practices
beats.text: II. A JUST WAR AGAINST IDOLATRY

narration.text: For the conquest: Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda. Scholar. Logician. He had never set foot in the Americas. Never seen a single person he was about to describe. [VOICE:sepulveda] Aristotle settled this two thousand years ago. Some peoples are slaves by nature: born to be ruled, unfit to govern themselves. Their idolatry, their human sacrifices: these offend nature itself. A war that ends such practices is not cruelty.

narration.text: So the debate changed nothing. And everything. Before Valladolid, no empire had formally asked whether winning a war could still make it wrong. Las Casas wrote the question down. The empire is gone. The question survived. [pause:2]
